## 1. Purpose

This SOP describes standardized procedures for tagging trees during
restoration field work at EA Program field sites. Tree tagging creates a
permanent, individual record for each tree so that management decisions
are consistent, repeatable, and transparent across field crews and over
time. A future student or technician should be able to revisit a tagged
tree and understand exactly why it was flagged and how its condition has
changed.

Tree tagging is used to:

- Identify which trees will be retained, removed, or monitored
- Track individual tree condition over time
- Create a permanent record for future groups and project documentation
- Support consistent decision-making across crew members

Recording a consistent set of fields for each individual tree allows
data to be combined, compared, and reused across projects and seasons
[@handley2021].


## 2. Scope

- **Applies to:** All EA Program field sites with tree cover, including
  riparian forest, oak woodland, mixed conifer stands, and planted trees
  at restoration and campus sites
- **Does not apply to:** Shrubs with DBH below 2.5 cm (use
  [SOP-F603](SOP-F603-vegetation-transect-surveys.qmd) for shrub cover);
  diameter, height, and plot-based inventory measurement (use
  [SOP-F604](SOP-F604-tree-dbh-forest-inventory.qmd)); timber cruising
  for commercial harvest; formal urban tree risk assessment, which
  requires a qualified arborist [@isa2017]
- **Location:** All EA Program terrestrial field sites with woody
  vegetation


## 3. Definitions

- **DBH (diameter at breast height):** The diameter of a tree trunk
  measured at 1.37 m (4.5 ft) above ground on the uphill side of the
  tree. The standard dimension for comparing tree sizes. Measurement
  procedure is defined in
  [SOP-F604](SOP-F604-tree-dbh-forest-inventory.qmd) [@avery2002;
  @usfs_fia2023].
- **Tag:** A numbered aluminum disk fastened to the tree. Each tag
  number is unique within the project.
- **Flagging:** Colored plastic tape tied loosely around a tree at eye
  level. Color communicates the management decision for that tree.
- **Condition rating:** A five-level score (Excellent, Good, Fair, Poor,
  Dead) describing tree health and structure.
- **Crown:** The upper part of a tree, including all branches and
  foliage.
- **Crown spread:** The average horizontal width of the crown, taken as
  the mean of the widest spread and a second spread measured at right
  angles to it [@americanforests2015].
- **Retain:** Leave the tree in place. Do not remove or damage.
- **Remove:** Tree is scheduled for cutting or restoration thinning.


## 4. Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                                          |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| PI / Field Lead   | Approve flag color codes before the season starts; review completed field forms and photo logs weekly; ensure the project meets restoration goals |
| Trained Personnel | Tag trees per this SOP; complete all fields in the tree assessment record; take required photos; flag trees correctly the first time |
| New Students      | Complete training before tagging independently          |

Minimum crew size is two persons at all times (safety requirement; see
[SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd)).


## 5. Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Overhead:** Dead branches and leaning or unstable trees (widow-makers)
  can fall without warning. Look up before approaching any tree. Do not
  work under or near hazard trees in high wind.
- **Sharp tools:** Hand saws, loppers, and pruners. Keep blades sheathed
  while walking, pass tools handle-first, and never carry open blades
  through brush.
- **Terrain, biota, and weather:** Uneven terrain, poison oak, ticks,
  snakes, stinging insects, and heat are common at EA field sites and
  are covered in [SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd).
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Hi-vis vest
- [ ] Closed-toed shoes or field boots
- [ ] Long sleeves and long pants (poison oak protection)
- [ ] Safety glasses or goggles
- [ ] Cut-resistant gloves (when using cutting tools)
- [ ] Hard hat (in areas with overhead hazard trees)
- [ ] Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)

### Emergency Procedures

Refer to [SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd) for stop-work
conditions, biotic and weather hazards, emergency contacts, and incident
response. Work in pairs at all times in forested areas.


## 6. Equipment and Materials

| Item                              | Notes                                       |
|:----------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------|
| Numbered aluminum tags            | Pre-numbered; one per tree                  |
| Aluminum or stainless nails       | For attaching tags; see Section 8.2 on growth allowance |
| Flagging tape (color set)         | Per the color codes in Section 7           |
| Diameter (DBH) tape               | Reads diameter directly in cm (pi tape)     |
| GPS unit or smartphone            | Record coordinates per [SOP-F006](SOP-F006-gps-site-navigation.qmd) |
| Camera or smartphone              | Minimum three photos per tree               |
| Field data sheets                 | Printed from Appendix A                      |
| Clipboard and pencils             | Pencils work better than pens in wet conditions |
| Long measuring tape               | For crown spread                            |
| Clinometer or laser rangefinder   | For tree height (optional); see [SOP-F604](SOP-F604-tree-dbh-forest-inventory.qmd) |
| Lumber crayon or paint marker     | For marking the DBH measurement point       |
| Hand saw or loppers (optional)    | For small branch clearance to access the trunk |


## 7. Flagging Color Codes

::: {.callout-important}
Confirm color codes with the crew and PI before working. Project-specific
changes must be documented in the field log.
:::

| Flag Color | Designation                                              |
|:-----------|:---------------------------------------------------------|
| ORANGE     | Confirmed removal: invasive species (primary target)     |
| YELLOW     | Confirmed removal: dead, dying, or hazard tree           |
| PINK       | Confirmed removal: restoration thinning                  |
| GREEN      | Retain: do not remove                                    |
| WHITE      | Under review: secondary evaluation required (do not remove yet) |
| RED        | Monitoring tree: reassess next cycle                     |
| BLUE       | Approved native for transplant or seed collection        |

**Rule:** Tie flagging loosely at eye level. Do not wrap tightly;
flagging can girdle the tree over time.


## 8. Procedure

### 8.1 Before Entering the Field (Daily Pre-Work)

Complete this checklist before leaving the vehicles each day:

- [ ] All PPE inspected and worn
- [ ] GPS units charged; project boundaries pre-loaded
- [ ] Tag number range assigned to each crew member (no duplicates)
- [ ] Communication check complete; phones functional
- [ ] Weather reviewed against the stop-work conditions in
      [SOP-F001](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd)
- [ ] Crew briefed: target species, flag color codes, today's objectives
- [ ] Cutting tools sharpened, sheathed, and inspected

### 8.2 Tree Tagging Step-by-Step

| Step | Action | Why it matters |
|:-----|:-------|:---------------|
| 1. Approach and evaluate | Assess tree form, lean, root zone, crown condition, and nearby hazards from more than one side before tagging | A tree that looks sound from one side may have rot, lean, or deadwood visible from another angle [@isa2017] |
| 2. Identify species | Confirm common and scientific name; cross-check against the project Invasive Priority List and Retain Species List. Use [SOP-F602 iNaturalist](SOP-F602-inaturalist.qmd) for ID support where needed | Tagging the wrong species leads to the wrong management decision |
| 3. Measure DBH | Measure at 1.37 m on the uphill side per [SOP-F604](SOP-F604-tree-dbh-forest-inventory.qmd) | DBH drives removal priority, allometric calculations, and monitoring frequency |
| 4. Assign flag color | Select the color per Section 7 and tie loosely at eye level | Color communicates the decision to every future crew member |
| 5. Install tag | Fasten the numbered tag on the uphill side at DBH height with a single aluminum or stainless nail. Leave the nail head protruding about 2 to 3 cm so the tree can grow without engulfing the tag | A consistent, accessible tag is easy to relocate and read in later seasons; leaving the nail proud accommodates radial growth and bark ingrowth [@usfs_fia2023] |
| 6. Photograph | Take at least three photos: (a) full tree form, (b) tag number close-up, (c) notable defects or hazards | Photos resolve disputes and provide evidence if a tag is lost |
| 7. Record data | Complete all fields in the tree assessment record (Appendix A) before moving to the next tree | If it is not written down, it did not happen |

::: {.callout-note}
### Crown spread (optional field)
If crown spread is recorded, measure the widest spread across the crown,
then measure a second spread at right angles to the first, and average
the two: (A + B) / 2 [@americanforests2015]. Tree height, if recorded,
is measured with a clinometer or laser rangefinder per
[SOP-F604](SOP-F604-tree-dbh-forest-inventory.qmd).
:::

### 8.3 Tree Condition Ratings

Use a consistent five-level scale. Note structural defects (lean,
cracks, cavities, deadwood, included bark) that influence the rating and
any hazard flag [@isa2017].

| Condition | Field indicators |
|:----------|:-----------------|
| EXCELLENT | No significant defects; vigorous, full crown; normal growth |
| GOOD      | Minor defects; healthy overall; normal growth               |
| FAIR      | Moderate defects; reduced vigor; some dieback               |
| POOR      | Major defects; significant dieback; structural risk         |
| DEAD      | No live tissue; standing snag or fallen log                 |


## 9. Quality Control

Perform these checks every tagging day:

1. **Tag uniqueness:** Confirm no tag number was used twice. Reconcile
   the day's tags against the assigned number ranges.
2. **Species cross-check:** Verify each species identification against
   the Invasive Priority and Retain Species lists. Flag uncertain IDs
   for review rather than guessing.
3. **Data completeness:** Confirm every tagged tree has a fully completed
   assessment record (Appendix A) with no blank required fields.
4. **Photo completeness (end of day):** Before leaving the site, scroll
   through the day's photos and confirm that every tag number has the
   three required photos (full form, tag close-up, defects). Re-photograph
   any tree that is missing photos before leaving.
5. **Second-observer check:** On a subset of trees (for example, 10%),
   have a second crew member independently confirm species, condition
   rating, and flag color. Resolve any disagreements with the field lead.

## 12. Training Record

Before tagging trees independently, each student or new technician must:

1. Read this SOP in full
2. Read [SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd) and pass a
   field safety check (PPE, stop-work conditions, emergency contacts)
3. Know the correct flag color codes
4. Demonstrate correct DBH measurement technique (per
   [SOP-F604](SOP-F604-tree-dbh-forest-inventory.qmd))
5. Correctly tag and flag three practice trees with the crew lead
   observing
6. Complete a tree assessment record without errors
7. Take an acceptable three-photo set (full tree, tag close-up, defects)
8. Be signed off by the PI or field lead

| Trainee | Date read SOP | Date practice trees | Signed off by | Date |
|:--------|:--------------|:--------------------|:--------------|:-----|
|         |               |                     |               |      |

## Appendix C: Field Note {.appendix}

This SOP is a field guide. It does not replace project permits or crew
